At the Sushi Restaurant

Quality checked lesson

Published 30 Sep 2026

Sushi restaurants let you order pieces at a counter or sit at a table. Knowing a few sushi words helps you ask what is available, choose food, make small requests, and pay.

Before you begin

Warm-Up Questions

  1. Do you like sushi?

    Need a starting line?

    There is no wrong answer.

  2. Do you prefer eating at the counter or at a table?

    Need a starting line?

    Both are common in sushi restaurants.

  3. What sushi piece do you know in English?

    Need a starting line?

    These are common piece names.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Some sushi restaurants have a sushi counter. You sit near the sushi chef and order piece by piece. Other places have tables. A server takes your order there. A simple start helps. Say hello. Ask what is good today. You can order a few pieces, or you can ask for a sushi set. Keep the first lines short so the chef or server can help you quickly.

Check your understanding

Check: How to Start

1. Name two ways to start an order at a sushi restaurant.

Sample answer

A clear start helps the chef or server help you.

Think one step further

Where do you like to sit in a sushi restaurant?

Useful language

Useful Phrases: How to Start

What is good today?
You ask which sushi is recommended now.What is good today? I want a few pieces.
Can I sit at the counter?
You ask to sit near the sushi chef.Can I sit at the counter, please?
I would like a few pieces, please.
A polite way to start a small order.I would like a few pieces, please.
Do you have a sushi set?
You ask for a fixed group of pieces.Do you have a sushi set for one person?

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Many people order nigiri, which is sushi rice with a topping. Common toppings are salmon, tuna, shrimp, and egg. Egg sushi is often called tamago. A cucumber roll is a simple maki roll with cucumber inside. Say the piece name clearly. Then say the count. For example: two pieces of salmon, please. Or: one cucumber roll, please. If you do not know a name, point and ask what it is. Short counts keep the order easy to hear.

Check: Pieces and Counts

1. Name three common sushi pieces and one way to order a count.

Sample answer

Clear piece names and counts help the chef.

Think one step further

Which piece would you order first?

Useful language

Useful Phrases: Pieces and Counts

Two pieces of salmon, please.
A clear count order for salmon sushi.Two pieces of salmon, please.
What is this one?
You ask about a piece you do not know.What is this one? Is it tuna?
One cucumber roll, please.
A polite order for a cucumber maki roll.One cucumber roll, please.
Is the shrimp cooked?
You ask a simple question about a dish.Is the shrimp cooked? I prefer cooked shrimp.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: After you choose pieces, you can make small requests. Say less wasabi or no wasabi if the paste is too hot. You can ask for ginger or soy sauce. Many people also ask for green tea. When you are finished, ask for the bill. Then say how you will pay. You can pay by card or with cash. Keep each request short so the server or sushi chef can confirm it.

Check: Requests and Paying

1. Name two small requests and one way to finish payment.

Sample answer

Short requests keep the order clear.

Think one step further

Do you usually pay by card or with cash?

Useful language

Useful Phrases: Requests and Paying

Less wasabi, please.
You ask for a smaller amount of wasabi.Less wasabi, please. It is strong for me.
No wasabi, please.
You ask to leave wasabi out.Two pieces of tuna, please. No wasabi, please.
Can I have the bill, please?
A polite way to ask to pay.Can I have the bill, please?
I will pay by card.
You say you will use a bank card.I will pay by card.

Roleplay: Order at the Counter

Kenji

You

You

Great. Two pieces of salmon, please.

Kenji

Two salmon. Anything else?

You

Yes. One tuna, please.

Kenji

One tuna. I will make them now.

You

Thank you.

Reading

Counter, Table, and How to Start

Some sushi restaurants have a sushi counter.

You sit near the sushi chef and order piece by piece.

Other places have tables.

A server takes your order there.

A simple start helps.

Say hello.

Ask what is good today.

You can order a few pieces, or you can ask for a sushi set.

Keep the first lines short so the chef or server can help you quickly.

Reading

Common Pieces and How to Order Counts

Many people order nigiri, which is sushi rice with a topping.

Common toppings are salmon, tuna, shrimp, and egg.

Egg sushi is often called tamago.

A cucumber roll is a simple maki roll with cucumber inside.

Say the piece name clearly.

Then say the count.

For example: two pieces of salmon, please.

Or: one cucumber roll, please.

If you do not know a name, point and ask what it is.

Short counts keep the order easy to hear.

Reading

Small Requests and Paying

After you choose pieces, you can make small requests.

Say less wasabi or no wasabi if the paste is too hot.

You can ask for ginger or soy sauce.

Many people also ask for green tea.

When you are finished, ask for the bill.

Then say how you will pay.

You can pay by card or with cash.

Keep each request short so the server or sushi chef can confirm it.
